title: Where before what
description: Why neurology looks for the lesion before it names the disease, and how that old method has to adapt when the nervous system being examined is still growing.
why: The site is named for a method, finding where the lesion is before asking what it is, and this module makes the case for that method.
objectives: Explain why clinical localization should come before imaging, and the four steps of neurologic diagnosis.
Name the eleven levels of the neuraxis and use findings to exclude levels.
Tell a destructive lesion from an irritative or releasing one by the direction of its signs.
Separate what the examination contributes (where) from what the history contributes (when).
Explain how localization sets the pretest probability that gives a scan, EEG or gene result its meaning.
Decide when several findings should be explained by one lesion and when by more than one.
Describe how development changes the meaning of findings in a child.

sections.title: The oldest rule
sections.content:
Long before neurology had a single effective treatment, it had a method, and that method is still the most distinctive thing it offers the rest of medicine. A cardiologist faced with a symptom can often reason straight to its cause, but a neurologist has to begin with a stranger question, which is *where* in this long, branching system something has gone wrong. The rule that follows is to **find the lesion before you name the disease**.

The question is an old one. The earliest surviving record of neurologic localization is an Egyptian surgical papyrus describing a man who could not answer questions after a wound to his temple (Brazis 2011, p. 1). In the nineteenth century Broca and Wernicke made the idea into a discipline by matching what patients could no longer do in life with what their brains showed at autopsy, which became the clinicopathologic method (Brazis 2011, pp. 1-2). Hughlings Jackson then added the warning that keeps the method honest. Finding the damage that abolishes a function is different from finding the function itself, because a lesion shows you where a circuit can be broken, and that is a different thing from where a faculty lives.

**The four steps**

Brazis and colleagues divide clinical diagnosis into four steps. You recognize that a function is impaired, decide which part of the nervous system is affected, list the likely causes, and only then use tests to choose among them (Brazis 2011, p. 2). Before the second step they pause over three preliminary questions, asking whether the deficit is real, whether it is pathological or one of life's ordinary aches, and whether it is neurologic at all or comes from a joint, a bone or a strained muscle (Brazis 2011, p. 3). Their advice on the first question is generous, since unless there are clear psychiatric features they suggest taking signs at face value.

**Why the scan comes second**

The order matters most when a scanner is involved, because imaging ordered without a localization finds things, and whatever it finds tends to get blamed. Brazis gives the example of congenital brain cysts, vivid on imaging, that were held responsible for symptoms they did not cause while the real disease went untreated (Brazis 2011, p. 1). Pearl and Emsellem come at the problem from the other side. Many diseases sit below the resolution of any scanner, so when the images and the patient disagree, the clinical picture has to be reconciled with the images rather than overruled by them (Pearl 2014, p. 1). Children sharpen the problem, because an incidental cyst or a small bright spot on MRI is common in childhood and frightening to parents, and only a localization made before the scan lets you tell them with confidence that *that is not the cause*.
keyPoints: Neurology's method is to find the lesion before naming the disease, asking where before asking what.
Brazis divides diagnosis into four steps, which are recognizing the impaired function, localizing it, listing the likely causes and then testing among them (Brazis 2011, p. 2).
Before localizing, ask whether the deficit is real, whether it is pathological and whether it is neurologic at all (Brazis 2011, p. 3).
Localize before imaging, because unlocalized scans find incidental lesions that then get blamed for the symptoms (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Hughlings Jackson warned that a lesion shows where a circuit can be broken, which is different from where a function lives.

question.question: A 9-year-old has two months of tripping over his left foot. An outside MRI of the brain, ordered for headache, shows a small arachnoid cyst. On examination he cannot lift or evert the left foot, but inversion and hip abduction are strong, and the rest of the exam is normal. What should guide the next step?
options: The cyst, because it is the only structural abnormality found so far
The localization from the exam, which points to the left common peroneal nerve, far from the cyst
A repeat brain MRI with contrast, to see whether the cyst is growing
A spine MRI, because foot drop always comes from the spinal cord
question.explanation: The examination has already localized the problem. Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with strong inversion and hip abduction is the pattern of a common peroneal nerve lesion, so the workup belongs there, with nerve studies and a search for compression at the fibular head. The cyst is exactly the kind of incidental finding Brazis warns will be blamed when imaging comes before localization, and a repeat brain MRI would only chase it to the wrong address. A spine MRI is reasonable in some children with foot drop, but here the spared inversion and hip abduction argue against an L5 root or cord lesion, and no rule says that foot drop always comes from the cord.

sections.title: The neuraxis is a list of addresses
sections.content:
Brazis compares finding a lesion to finding a house, which you can locate either by its street number or by the intersection of two streets (Brazis 2011, p. 3). Either way you need a map with named stops, and this curriculum uses eleven of them, running from the top down through the **cerebral cortex, subcortex and deep gray matter, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, anterior horn cell, nerve root, plexus, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle.** Every weakness, numbness or clumsiness you will ever examine lives at one or more of these addresses.

The worked example in Brazis shows how an intersection pins a lesion down. A third-nerve palsy on its own could sit anywhere along the nerve's long course, but once a hemiparesis appears on the opposite side, only one place carries both the third-nerve fibers and the corticospinal tract, and that is the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain on the side of the palsy (Brazis 2011, pp. 3-4).

**Use the figure above as an elimination game.** Each finding you switch on removes the levels that cannot produce it and tells you why they went, and the presets give you some ready-made patterns to start from. Weakness of the face along with the arm and leg removes the spinal cord at once, because the cord has no face. A sensory level on the trunk removes every level except the cord. As you play, you will find that a finding is most useful when it *excludes* a level, far more than when it merely fits one.

**Precision falls as you climb**

Brazis observes that localization is most precise low in the nervous system and least precise in the cortex (Brazis 2011, p. 4). A muscle lesion weakens that muscle, and a nerve lesion weakens its muscles and numbs its skin, but a cortical lesion produces a shifting array of motor, sensory and behavioral findings. Low-level signs are also *consistent*, so wasting of a hand muscle is there every time you look. Higher-level signs can come and go during a single examination, which is why, for language and other higher functions, the useful question is whether the patient performs a task consistently and normally rather than whether they can manage it once (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

The gradient has a practical edge in children. A toddler's cortex-level skills, such as language, attention and praxis, are still being built and have to be measured against age, whereas the motor unit already behaves much as it will in adulthood, so the lower the level you are examining, the more you can trust a single clean sign.
keyPoints: The curriculum's eleven addresses are the cortex, subcortex, brainstem, cerebellum, cord, anterior horn, root, plexus, nerve, junction and muscle.
A lesion is often found where two damaged pathways intersect, as when a third-nerve palsy with an opposite hemiparesis places it in the midbrain (Brazis 2011, pp. 3-4).
Findings are most useful when they exclude levels, so localization works largely by elimination.
Localization is most precise low in the neuraxis and least precise in the cortex, where signs may be inconsistent (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

question.question: A 15-year-old develops, over one morning, a drooping right eyelid with the right eye turned down and out and a dilated right pupil, together with weakness of the left arm and leg. Where is the single lesion most likely to be?
options: The left internal capsule
The right oculomotor nerve in the orbit
The left side of the pons
The right cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
question.explanation: The lesion has to sit where both damaged pathways run together. The right third-nerve fibers and the corticospinal fibers for the left limbs, which have not yet crossed, travel together only in the right cerebral peduncle, the textbook intersection Brazis uses. A left capsular lesion would weaken the right limbs and spare the eye. A third-nerve lesion in the orbit explains the eye but leaves the hemiparesis unexplained. A left pontine lesion would weaken the right limbs and, if it involved a cranial nerve, would affect a pontine nerve on the left rather than the right third nerve.

sections.title: Lesions that go quiet, and lesions that fire
sections.content:
Picture two children in the same emergency department on the same night, both with their eyes pulled hard to the left. The first, a seven-year-old, has a twitching left cheek and a left hand jerking in rhythm. The second, a teenager brought in from football practice, is lying still, and his right arm is heavy and weak. If you went by the eyes alone, you would put both problems in the same place, and you would be wrong about one of them.

The explanation lies in how the frontal eye fields work. Each one pushes the eyes toward the opposite side, and at rest the two pushes cancel out. When one field is destroyed, as in a stroke, its partner pushes without opposition and the eyes drift toward the damaged side (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 43). When one field fires, as in a seizure, it overpowers its partner and drives the eyes away from itself (Pearl 2014, p. 9). DeMyer adds a detail that is easy to miss at the bedside, which is that once the seizure ends and the exhausted focus falls quiet, the eyes can swing back the other way (DeMyer, p. 182). So the girl has a right frontal focus that is firing, and the teenager has a left-sided lesion that has stopped working.

That difference, between tissue that has gone quiet and tissue that is working too hard, runs through the whole nervous system. Pearl and Emsellem credit Hughlings Jackson with insisting that the nervous system could be understood as a sensorimotor machine, with nothing mysterious in the wiring (Pearl 2014, p. 10), and the machine comparison earns its keep here. When a part simply stops, neurologists speak of **negative signs**, such as a weak hand, a blind half of the visual field or a patch of numb skin. When a part runs too hard, the signs are **positive**, like the jerking hand or the eyes driven sideways. The vagus nerve shows both faces, since irritating it slows the heart and destroying it lets the heart race (Pearl 2014, p. 56).

DeMyer describes a third possibility, which he calls **release** (DeMyer, p. 292). Some parts of the nervous system exist largely to hold other parts back, and when they fail, whatever they were restraining becomes more active. That is why a child with an upper motor neuron lesion has brisk reflexes, clonus, rising tone and an upgoing toe. The lower motor neuron is intact, and nothing is supervising it anymore (Pearl 2014, pp. 65, 108). The palmar grasp shows the same idea across a lifetime. In a newborn it is normal and fades over the first months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/introduction.html)), but in an older patient whose frontal lobes are failing, the same grasp can come back, and now it counts as a **frontal release sign** (Pearl 2014, p. 114).

There is a fourth and stranger possibility. When an input is lost, the brain does not always notice the gap. A patient blinded by damage to both occipital lobes may insist that they can see, and will describe things that are not there (Pearl 2014, p. 29). A patient with a right parietal lesion may say that a paralyzed left arm is moving normally, a condition Babinski named **anosognosia** (DeMyer, p. 441). In both cases the brain supplies a confident account in the place where the function used to be, which is why a patient's own report can mislead in ways that are themselves localizing.

The figure above sorts these four possibilities by structure. Choose one and look at which kinds of sign it can produce; you will find that irritation often points in the opposite direction from destruction, and that only some structures release or fill in.
keyPoints: A lesion can subtract function (negative signs), irritate tissue (positive signs), release what it used to restrain, or leave the brain to fill the gap.
When a frontal eye field is destroyed the eyes look toward the lesion, and when it fires in a seizure they are driven away from it (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 43).
Brisk reflexes, clonus and an upgoing toe are release signs, produced when the lower motor neuron is freed from restraint (Pearl 2014, pp. 65, 108; DeMyer, p. 292).
The newborn's palmar grasp is a normal milestone, but the same grasp returning later in frontal disease is a release sign (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam; Pearl 2014, p. 114).
Denied blindness and denied paralysis are examples of the brain filling in for a lost input (Pearl 2014, p. 29; DeMyer, p. 441).

question.question: A 7-year-old who was well at breakfast is brought in mid-event: her head and eyes are forced to the left, and her left face and arm are jerking rhythmically. Where is the lesion, and what is it doing?
options: The left frontal lobe, destroyed, so the eyes look toward the damaged side
The right pons, destroyed, so the eyes look away from it
The left frontal lobe, firing, so the eyes turn toward the focus
The right frontal lobe, firing, so the eyes are driven away from the focus
question.explanation: Rhythmic jerking is a positive, irritative sign, and the company it keeps settles where the eyes are pointing. A right frontal seizure drives the eyes to the left while the right motor cortex jerks the left face and arm (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 104). A destroyed left frontal eye field also leaves the eyes looking left, which makes it tempting, but destruction subtracts function and would bring a still, weak right side rather than a jerking left one. A right pontine lesion turns the eyes left too, yet produces no jerking. A left-sided focus would drive the eyes to the right and jerk the right limbs. Once the seizure ends, the eyes may drift briefly to the right as the exhausted focus goes quiet (DeMyer, p. 182).

sections.title: Dividing the work between examination and history
sections.content:
Students tend to assume that a good history will tell them where the lesion is, and they are often surprised by how neurologists actually divide the labor. For finding *where*, Brazis says, the examination is far more important than the history, and a lesion can often be localized from the examination alone. Brazis even counts the sensory findings a patient reports during the exam as examination data, so a complaint of numbness can be as objective as a wrist drop (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

What the history contributes, above all, is **time**. Brazis's example is a left hemiparesis found on examination, which suggests a vascular event or a seizure if it arrived over minutes, infection or demyelination if it evolved over a few days, and a tumor or a degenerative process if it crept in over months (Brazis 2011, p. 4). The examination places the lesion, and the tempo suggests what kind of lesion it is. That pairing of *where* from the exam with *when* from the story is the backbone of the whole curriculum, and [[m11-where-to-what|Module 11]] builds it into a working differential.

**Three questions at the bedside**

Morris and Jankovic close every examination by asking where the lesion is, what the phenomenology is, and what the likely underlying cause is. They pair those questions with advice worth taping to the wall, which is to commit yourself to a diagnosis, with a short differential if you must, instead of listing every possible cause for fear of being wrong, since if you prove wrong you will have learned something (Morris 2012, p. xxix). They also note that neurology is unusual among the specialties in relying on localization, or on recognition of the phenomenon, before it can reach a cause (Morris 2012, p. xxv). The middle question earns its place with disorders that have no focal lesion at all. A tremor, a seizure type or a tic is recognized by what it looks like, and in those disorders recognition takes over the job that localization does elsewhere.

**When in a child**

Children add a second clock, because besides asking "how long has this been happening?" you also need to ask "since when in development?" A weakness present since early infancy, a skill that never arrived, and a skill that was there and has since been lost are three different stories, even when today's examination looks the same in all of them, and the last section of this module returns to that idea.
keyPoints: For localization the examination matters more than the history, and sensory findings the patient reports during the exam count as examination data (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
The history supplies the tempo, with minutes suggesting a vascular event or seizure, days suggesting infection or demyelination, and months suggesting tumor or degeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Morris and Jankovic end every exam by asking where the lesion is, what the phenomenology is and what the cause is, and they advise committing to a diagnosis (Morris 2012, p. xxix).
In a child, also ask since when in development, and distinguish skills never acquired, static deficits and skills that have been lost.

question.question: A 12-year-old girl has a left hemiparesis on examination. Her parents say her left hand has become gradually clumsier over the last five months and she has started to drag her left foot. Which group of causes should head your list?
options: A tumor or a slowly progressive process
An arterial ischemic stroke
A focal seizure with post-ictal weakness
Guillain-Barré syndrome
question.explanation: The examination gives the place, a lesion of the right hemisphere or of the descending motor pathway, and the history gives the tempo. Steady progression over months points first to a tumor or another slowly progressive process (Brazis 2011, p. 4). A stroke and a seizure with post-ictal weakness both arrive over minutes, so neither fits a story that has unfolded over five months. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a peripheral, usually symmetric disorder that evolves over days to weeks, and it would not produce a hemiparesis.

sections.title: The exam as a prior: scans, EEGs and genes
sections.content:
Suppose two ten-year-olds have EEGs on the same afternoon, and both reports describe focal epileptiform discharges. The first has seizures that turn her eyes to the left and jerk her left face and hand, the signature of a right frontal focus, and that is where her discharges sit. The second has headaches and a normal examination, and his EEG was ordered to be thorough. In the first child the report confirms a prediction the examination had already made, and in the second it arrives with nothing to confirm.

The arithmetic that explains the difference also explains section 1's innocent cyst, and it is the strongest argument for the whole doctrine. A test moves a belief by an amount that depends on where the belief started. Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century British vicar and amateur mathematician, gave the movement the form clinicians use daily without naming it, **pretest odds × likelihood ratio = post-test odds**. Gill and colleagues call a test an "opinion modifier" ([Gill 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15879401/)), and the uncomfortable corollary is that an identical report means different things in different children, because it lands on different priors.

**The exam sets the prior**

Every localization is a prediction, whether it puts the lesion in the right frontal lobe, the left peroneal nerve or somewhere no scanner can see. A finding at the predicted address inherits the exam's weight, while one at an address the exam excluded starts near zero and needs overwhelming evidence. Brazis puts clinical diagnosis ahead of ancillary tests for exactly this reason, since the false positives of "gunshot" imaging are avoided only by careful localization (Brazis 2011, p. 1). The second child's discharges have no prediction behind them, so their meaning depends on how often healthy children show the same thing.

**What healthy children's tests show**

The base rates are larger than the word "healthy" suggests. Research MRI of 9- and 10-year-olds found incidental findings in 21.1%, most needing no referral ([Li 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33749724/)), and epileptiform discharges, the very finding on the second child's report, appeared in 6.5% of healthy 6- to 13-year-olds ([Borusiak 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20002145/)). Ordinary background fluctuations such as sharply contoured rhythms and fragmented alpha are also overread as epileptiform, which helps sustain a wrong diagnosis of epilepsy ([Benbadis 2003](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12684557/)). Gene reports grade variants on five tiers from benign to pathogenic, with **uncertain significance** in the middle ([Richards 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25741868/)). A variant of uncertain significance is not a positive result, and whether it matters depends on how well the child matches what the gene does, which is a question for the exam.

**Scan versus story**

The mismatch between test and patient runs both ways. Much disease lies below the resolution of imaging, and the scan and the clinical picture can simply disagree (Pearl 2014, p. 1). A child weak from disease of nerve or neuromuscular junction has a normal brain MRI because the disease is not in the brain, so the normal scan acquits nothing, and by the same logic an abnormal scan convicts nothing unless the exam put the lesion there.

**Use the figure above** by choosing a test and then a prior. The false-positive rates are sourced and the priors illustrative. Hold the result fixed while you move the prior, and the meaning of the same positive report rises and falls with the exam.

> **Rule of thumb.** After the history and examination, choose the one or two tests most likely to confirm or refute the tentative diagnosis, rather than every test that might turn something up (DeMyer, p. 539).
keyPoints: A test modifies an opinion, and in odds form the pretest odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio give the post-test odds (Gill 2005).
The localization sets the pretest probability, so a finding where the exam predicted it means far more than one at an address the exam excluded (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Healthy children often have abnormal-looking tests, with incidental MRI findings in 21.1% at 9 to 10 years (Li 2021) and epileptiform discharges in 6.5% at 6 to 13 years (Borusiak 2010).
A variant of uncertain significance is not a positive result, and the child's phenotype decides how much weight it carries (Richards 2015).
A normal scan cannot clear disease below the resolution of imaging, and an abnormal one cannot convict without the exam (Pearl 2014, p. 1).

question.question: An 11-year-old has fainted three times in a year, each time after standing in a hot school assembly: she felt lightheaded, her vision grayed out, she slumped, and she was herself again within a minute. Her examination is normal. A routine EEG reports a few focal epileptiform discharges. What do the discharges most likely mean?
options: They prove the episodes are focal seizures, so treatment for epilepsy should start
They make syncope and epilepsy equally likely, so both should be treated
They outweigh the history, because an EEG is objective and a story is not
They are most likely a trait that some healthy children carry, and the story still points to fainting
question.explanation: The history sets a low prior for epilepsy. Episodes provoked by standing in the heat, with graying vision, a slump and rapid recovery, are the story of a vasovagal or orthostatic faint, which Pearl lists among the mimics of epilepsy (Pearl 2014, p. 104). Because epileptiform discharges occur in 6.5% of healthy 6- to 13-year-olds (Borusiak 2010), a positive EEG moves that low prior only a little. Treating the discharges as proof of seizures is the tempting error, since even an objective test needs a prior, and the tracing itself deserves a second look because normal fluctuations are overread (Benbadis 2003). The result does not make the two diagnoses equally likely, and treating both would mean treating a test result instead of the child.

sections.title: One lesion or many
sections.content:
Faced with several abnormal findings, the localizer's first instinct is parsimony, which means looking for **one lesion that explains them all.** The instinct is usually right, and it drives the intersection method, since a third-nerve palsy and a hemiparesis are far more likely to come from one midbrain lesion than from two unrelated ones.

Parsimony is still only a strategy, and nature doesn't promise to follow it. Medicine has a famous counterweight to Occam's razor, usually attributed to John Hickam, which holds that patients can have as many diseases as they please. A clinical problem-solving case in the *New England Journal of Medicine* sets Occam's razor against **Saint's triad**, the observation that some patients genuinely carry several unrelated conditions at once ([Hilliard 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14762188/)). The skill lies in recognizing when to stop forcing a single explanation onto findings that resist it.

**Time is the referee**

Brazis offers the cleanest test, using the same pair of findings. A third-nerve palsy and a hemiparesis that appear together point to the midbrain. If the palsy dates from childhood and the hemiparesis appeared decades later, though, the hemiparesis probably did not come from a midbrain lesion at all, and the examination is showing the end result of two lesions that arrived at different times (Brazis 2011, p. 4). So the history matters for localization as well as for cause, and before you weld findings into one lesion it is worth asking whether they began together.

**Discrete lesions and system lesions**

Brazis also distinguishes two kinds of damage. Most localization teaching is built on **discrete lesions**, such as an infarct, a demyelinating plaque, a tumor or an abscess, each of which damages everything in one place. Other diseases attack a **functional system** instead, meaning an array of related neurons scattered across several levels (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Parkinson disease localizes neatly to the substantia nigra, whereas a spinocerebellar degeneration does not sit at one address at all. When findings refuse to settle at one level, it helps to consider in turn whether there are several discrete lesions (as in demyelinating disease), a diffuse toxic or metabolic process, or a system degeneration. [[m10-everywhere|Module 10]] takes up the case where the answer is "everywhere".

The question takes a particular form in children. A child with a static motor disability from early life can acquire a new and unrelated problem, and the old findings have to be subtracted before the new ones can be localized, which makes asking the parents about the child's baseline part of the localization itself.
keyPoints: Start with parsimony and try to explain all the findings with one lesion.
Occam's razor has counterweights in Hickam's dictum and Saint's triad, because a patient can have more than one disease (Hilliard 2004).
Findings that began at different times may come from different lesions, so the time course decides whether to merge them (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Discrete lesions differ from system disorders, which affect related neurons across several levels (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
In a child with a pre-existing disability, establish the baseline before localizing the new problem.

question.question: A 14-year-old with spastic diplegia since infancy (born preterm) now has three weeks of tingling and weakness creeping up from both feet, and his previously brisk ankle reflexes are now absent. What is the best way to think about the localization?
options: His long-standing diplegia explains everything, so no new localization is needed
The new findings must come from the same old brain lesion, which must be progressing
Two problems at two addresses: an old central lesion and a new peripheral one, which must be localized on its own
Reflexes are unreliable in cerebral palsy, so the change can be ignored
question.explanation: His baseline is a static central lesion, which produces brisk reflexes. A new ascending sensory and motor disturbance with loss of those reflexes is a change in kind that points to a new peripheral process such as a polyneuropathy, and it has to be localized on its own. Forcing everything onto the old diagnosis misapplies parsimony, because the findings began at different times (Brazis 2011, p. 4). A static brain lesion does not make reflexes disappear, and dismissing a change in reflexes in a child with cerebral palsy is exactly how a second diagnosis gets missed.

sections.title: The child is a moving target
sections.content:
An adult's nervous system holds still while you examine it, but a child's keeps changing as you watch, which makes **development the fourth dimension of pediatric localization**. The same finding can be normal at one age and a sign of disease at another, and a fixed lesion can produce signs that change as the brain around it grows.

**When age changes the meaning**

The upgoing big toe is a good place to start. It is a cornerstone sign of corticospinal tract damage, yet it is normal in the first year of life, while the corticospinal tracts are still being myelinated ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)), and DeMyer notes that the closer an infant is to one year, the more consistently the toe goes down (DeMyer, p. 282). Handedness runs the opposite way. Preferring one hand is unremarkable in an adult, but in an infant it is a red flag, because a hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/06month.html)). The baby who reaches only with the right hand is telling you about the left.

**A lesion that stays put while its signs change**

Cerebral palsy is defined as a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture attributed to **non-progressive** disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain ([Rosenbaum 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17370477/)). Although the lesion does not grow, the clinical picture does, and DeMyer points out that infants with cerebral palsy may first appear hypotonic before spasticity evolves (DeMyer, p. 273). So a floppy infant who becomes a stiff toddler need not have a progressive disease, because the lesion was there all along and the maturing motor system has revealed it.

**Localization in time**

In children, then, you localize along a time axis as well as a spatial one, and part of the work is deciding which of three stories the child is in.
- **Static** problems are present from early life and not worsening, though their expression may change with growth.
- **Progressive** problems are getting worse, which demands a search for an active process.
- **Regressive** problems involve the loss of skills once acquired, the most urgent pattern of all, because it implies the nervous system is being damaged now.

No single examination can tell these three apart, but the history, the developmental record and repeated examinations can, which is why in child neurology the second visit is often more informative than the first.
keyPoints: Development is the fourth dimension of pediatric localization, because the meaning of a finding depends on the child's age.
An upgoing toe is normal in the first year while the corticospinal tracts myelinate (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Cerebral palsy comes from a non-progressive lesion, yet its signs evolve, and hypotonia may come before spasticity (Rosenbaum 2007; DeMyer, p. 273).
Classify the time course as static, progressive or regressive, and treat regression as the most urgent.

question.question: At a 9-month check, a mother says her baby always reaches with the right hand and seems to ignore toys offered on the left. The baby is otherwise well and sitting. What is the right interpretation and next step?
options: Early right-handedness, a normal variant; reassure
A possible left hemiparesis; examine carefully for asymmetry of tone, reflexes and the parachute response, and arrange brain imaging if confirmed
A visual problem in the left eye; refer to ophthalmology only
A sign of autism; refer for developmental assessment
question.explanation: Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the non-preferred hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam), so this baby should be examined for a left hemiparesis, which in an infant often follows a perinatal stroke and localizes to the right hemisphere. Calling it early handedness offers false reassurance. A visual field or eye problem can make a baby ignore one side, and vision is worth checking, but referring only to ophthalmology skips the more likely motor explanation. Nothing in the history points to autism, and that label would delay the motor workup.

quiz.question: A medical student, keen to be efficient, orders a brain MRI on every child with a new neurologic complaint before examining them. Which step of clinical diagnosis has been skipped, and what is the main risk?
options: Recognition of impaired function; the risk is missing the diagnosis entirely
Listing likely causes; the risk is ordering too few tests
Localization; the risk is that incidental findings get blamed for the symptoms while the real lesion is missed
Ancillary testing; the risk is radiation exposure
quiz.explanation: Brazis places localization second of four steps, after recognizing the impaired function and before listing causes or ordering tests (Brazis 2011, p. 2), and warns that unlocalized imaging produces false positives such as congenital cysts blamed for unrelated symptoms (Brazis 2011, p. 1). Recognition of impaired function has still happened, since the child came with a complaint. Listing causes and ordering tests have not been skipped so much as done too early. MRI involves no ionizing radiation, so radiation exposure is not the risk here.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has a right sixth-nerve palsy that began suddenly last week. His mother mentions that his left leg has dragged since a bicycle accident when he was 6. How should these two findings be localized?
options: As one right pontine lesion, because a sixth-nerve palsy with a contralateral leg weakness is a crossed brainstem syndrome
As probably two separate problems, because they began ten years apart
As one left hemisphere lesion, because the leg is on the left
The leg weakness should be ignored because it is old
quiz.explanation: A crossed pattern points to the brainstem only when the findings began together. When deficits arrive years apart, the examination may be showing two lesions, which is the point of Brazis's third-nerve example (Brazis 2011, p. 4), and merging them into one pontine lesion misapplies parsimony. A left hemisphere lesion would weaken the right leg rather than the left. Nor should the old weakness be ignored, since it is part of the baseline that any new localization has to account for.

quiz.question: On a busy ward round, a resident examines a 7-year-old with a headache and documents only 'neuro exam WNL'. What is the problem with this note?
options: Nothing, if the child is well
It should say 'non-focal' instead
It records a conclusion instead of what was actually tested and found, so no one can tell what was examined
It should include a numerical score such as the Glasgow Coma Scale
quiz.explanation: A recorded examination exists so that the next reader can see what was tested and what was found, and 'within normal limits' hides both. DeMyer explicitly rejects 'WNL' as a record of the examination (DeMyer, p. 604) and asks for objective recording before interpretation (DeMyer, p. 36). Writing 'non-focal' has the same flaw. A coma score has no bearing on a well, alert child and would not fix the problem.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old with a new speech problem repeats some phrases perfectly and fails on others of similar difficulty. What should the examiner conclude about repetition?
options: Repetition is normal, because he can do it
Repetition is impaired, because higher functions should be judged by whether they are consistently normal
The test is invalid in children and should not be recorded
He is not trying, so the finding is functional
quiz.explanation: Brazis notes that signs from higher levels of the nervous system can be inconsistent within one examination, and that the right question is whether the patient performs a task consistently and normally, rather than whether they can do it once (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Recording repetition as normal because some phrases succeed misses the deficit. Repetition can certainly be tested in a 10-year-old. Inconsistency at higher levels is expected in organic disease, so on its own it does not point to a functional disorder.

quiz.question: An 8-month-old born at term has an upgoing big toe on both sides when the sole is stroked. The rest of the examination, development and tone are normal. What does the plantar response mean?
options: It is consistent with normal development at this age
It localizes to the spinal cord and needs urgent imaging
It localizes to both cerebral hemispheres
It shows a peripheral nerve problem
quiz.explanation: An upgoing toe is normal in the first year of life while the corticospinal tracts myelinate (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam), and DeMyer notes that the flexor response becomes more constant as the infant approaches one year (DeMyer, p. 282). In a developmentally normal 8-month-old with symmetric findings it is not a localizing sign, so it points neither to the spinal cord nor to both hemispheres, although reproducible asymmetry would be a different matter. A peripheral nerve lesion cannot produce an extensor plantar response at any age.

quiz.question: Three children each have a weak left leg today. In the first it has been the same since birth; in the second it has worsened over a year; in the third a child who was walking normally has stopped walking over two months. Which child needs the most urgent workup, and why?
options: The first, because congenital problems are the most severe
All three equally, since today's examinations are identical
The third, because loss of an acquired skill implies the nervous system is being damaged now
The second, because slow progression always means a tumor
quiz.explanation: Regression, the loss of a skill once acquired, implies an active process damaging the nervous system now, and it is the most urgent of the three time courses. The deficit present since birth fits a fixed early lesion. The slowly progressive deficit also needs investigation, but slow progression has several possible causes and does not always mean a tumor. Identical examinations on one day do not make the three stories equivalent, because in children the time axis is part of the localization.

quiz.question: Two children have identical MRI reports describing a small area of abnormal signal in the left frontal lobe. The first has had focal seizures with jerking of the right arm and now a weak right hand. The second was scanned for headaches and has a normal examination. How should the same finding be weighed in each?
options: It is far more likely to be the cause in the first child, because the exam predicted a lesion at that address
It means the same in both, because the reports are identical
It is more likely to matter in the second child, because a normal exam cannot rule a lesion out
Neither can be interpreted until a repeat scan shows whether it changes
quiz.explanation: The reports are identical but the priors are not. In the first child the exam localized to the left motor cortex before the scan, so the finding lands on a high pretest probability and is very likely the cause, since post-test odds are the pretest odds multiplied by the test's likelihood ratio (Gill 2005). In the second child nothing predicted a lesion there, and incidental findings appear in 21.1% of research MRIs in 9- to 10-year-olds (Li 2021). Treating the reports as equivalent ignores the prior. A normal exam does not raise the chance that a finding matters, and while a repeat scan may be reasonable later, it does not replace the reasoning now.

signOff: On three real patients, the resident states the level of the lesion before ordering imaging, and a faculty member agrees.

opener.parable: Imagine posting a letter with the right name on the envelope but no street or town. It isn't exactly lost, but nobody can deliver it until someone works out where it should go. A child's symptoms often arrive in clinic in the same state, and many of the tests we reach for are really attempts to guess the address.
opener.history: The oldest localization on record comes from Egypt, where a surgeon writing more than four thousand years ago described a man with a wound in the temple who could not answer when spoken to. Much later, the Hippocratic physicians recorded that an injury to the left side of the brain weakens the right side of the body.
